title: Cell refreshes itself: storage-gated keeper on a pulsed restore rail
idea: Reverse who refreshes: instead of the periphery sensing and rewriting row by row, add a tiny second transistor to each cell whose gate is the storage node and whose channel links the node to a shared restore rail. Pulsing the rail to a boosted level (about VARY+Vt) tops up only cells still holding a '1' (their keeper is on) while '0' cells stay off, so one array-wide pulse refreshes millions of cells with no sense amps, no bitline swing and no bank lockout.
why: Refresh energy and time (fact 3): ~46 fJ/bit refresh shrinks to the few-fJ CV top-up of decayed charge, and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss goes to ~0; costs ~30-40% more cell area (2T1C).

title: Inverted HBM: logic die on top, DRAM tiers below
idea: Rearrange the stack order: put the hot base/logic die at the top of the stack, directly under the heatsink, and the DRAM tiers beneath it on the interposer, with logic power fed up through a dedicated power-via column in the DRAM dies. DRAM no longer sits in the heat path of the logic die.
why: Leakage roughly doubles every ~10 C; DRAM running 15-25 C cooler cuts refresh rate 2-4x and leaves the >85 C double-refresh range (facts 3, 6).

title: Capacitor-first, transistor-last cell with high-temperature dielectric anneal
idea: Reverse the process order: build and crystallize the storage capacitor first (rutile TiO2 or SrTiO3 annealed at 700-800 C for k~70-100), then bond a thin single-crystal Si layer on top and form the access transistor with laser or microwave anneal so the capacitor is never reheated. The transistor never sees the capacitor's thermal budget, and the capacitor never has to tolerate the transistor's.
why: Charge wall (fact 1) and retention (fact 3): k~70+ gives ~2x Cs at today's aspect ratio, and a top-side transistor has no storage-node-to-substrate junction; ~2-4x longer refresh interval.

title: Turn GIDL into the switch: band-to-band tunnel-FET access device
idea: Reverse the role of the worst leakage mechanism: GIDL is band-to-band tunneling at the gate edge, so make that the ON mechanism with a p-i-n tunnel-FET access device (SiGe/Ge source pocket at the bitline end). The off state has no thermionic path, giving aA-level off current and sub-60 mV/dec swing, and DRAM tolerates the TFET's low on-current because a 5 fF cell needs only ~1-5 uA to write in a few ns.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): off current 100-1000x below the ~13 fA tail could stretch retention from 64 ms to seconds; the smaller wordline swing also eases the voltage floor (fact 10).

title: Store the majority in the leak-sink state with row inversion flags
idea: Flip data polarity per row: at each write, on-die logic counts the bits and stores the row inverted whenever that places more bits in the discharged state the cells leak toward, recording one flag bit per 1 KB row. Zero-heavy real data then keeps 80-90% of bits in a state that cannot decay.
why: Refresh (fact 3): only charged cells can fail, so per-row failure probability drops 5-10x and the refresh interval stretches ~2-4x at the same ECC strength; <0.1% bit overhead.

title: Refresh scan turns uniform rows into a single metadata bit
idea: Reverse refresh from a pure cost into a survey: as the refresh engine senses each row, a small comparator in the sense-amp stripe detects rows that are all-0 or all-1 and sets a bit in a per-subarray bitmap. Those rows drop out of the refresh schedule and their contents are regenerated from the bitmap when next opened.
why: Refresh energy/time (fact 3): zeroed and freed pages are often 20-50% of server DRAM, so refresh energy and idle power fall by a similar share.

title: Floating segment node: cells leak into neighbors, not the bitline
idea: Rearrange the isolation hierarchy: group 4-8 cells on a short local node that connects to the bitline through one segment transistor. In hold the segment device is off, so the local node floats and settles between the cells' stored voltages; each access transistor sees a small Vds, and any path to the bitline must cross two off devices in series (stack effect).
why: Subthreshold leakage (fact 3) falls ~5-10x via stack effect and reduced Vds/DIBL, stretching refresh ~3-5x; the segment switch also cuts bitline load per access.

title: Micro-sense: one local amplifier per 16 cells
idea: Reverse the cell-to-amplifier ratio: instead of ~500 cells on a long bitline per sense amp, place a 3-4 transistor local preamp (CMOS under array) under every 16-cell local bitline, so bitline capacitance drops from ~50 fF to ~3 fF. The transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+Cbl) rises from ~0.1 to ~0.6, so a cell stays readable after losing far more of its charge.
why: Retention margin (facts 1, 3): tolerating 3-5x more charge loss lengthens refresh 3-5x at the same leakage, or permits a ~2 fF capacitor instead of chasing AR 115.

title: Antiferroelectric latent-charge buffer holds stored-1 voltage on a plateau
idea: Reverse the capacitor dielectric's role from passive to defending its charge: use ZrO2-rich antiferroelectric HZO and bias the plate so a stored '1' sits just above the AFE back-switching voltage. As leakage drains the node, AFE domains switch back and release bound polarization charge (~10-20 uC/cm2), pinning the voltage on a plateau the way latent heat holds ice water at 0 C.
why: Retention and charge wall (facts 1, 3): effective capacitance at the hold point rises 5-10x, so retention rises ~5x without taller pillars; AFE has no remanent polarization, avoiding the fatigue/imprint of prior HZO FeRAM concepts.

title: Mechanical switch: vertical NEMS contact replaces the access transistor
idea: Reverse what moves: instead of gating electrons through a semiconductor, the wordline electrostatically pulls a ~10 nm-gap vertical nanocantilever (Ru- or TiN-coated) into contact with the storage node. When open the gap is vacuum or gas, so off-state leakage is essentially zero and retention is limited only by capacitor dielectric leakage (minutes to hours).
why: Eliminates the access-transistor leakage tail and refresh (fact 3) and allows a low actuation voltage via nanogap; contact endurance of ~1e15 cycles is the core risk.

title: Empty the channel: nano-vacuum field-emission access device
idea: Remove the semiconductor from the switch: the storage node faces a sharpened emitter tip across a sealed ~5-10 nm vacuum gap, and the wordline acts as an extraction gate. With the gate low there are no carriers in the gap, so leakage is only direct tunneling through vacuum; with the gate high, Fowler-Nordheim field emission conducts uA currents in picoseconds.
why: Access-device leakage (fact 3) essentially removed and retention no longer set by thermal generation, so refresh stops scaling with temperature; risks are emitter stability and gate voltage.

title: Junctionless storage node removes the leakage-tail junction
idea: Reverse the doping layout: make the access device a uniformly n-doped ultrathin (<=5 nm) junctionless channel that turns off by full depletion under a wraparound gate, so there is no n+/p metallurgical junction at the storage node. Trap-assisted junction leakage and junction-field GIDL, the main sources of the retention tail and variable retention time, lose their high-field region.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): removing the storage-node junction field could cut tail leakage ~10x and shrink VRT, relaxing refresh ~4-8x.

title: Thin to widen: quantum-confined 2 nm channel raises effective bandgap
idea: Reverse the scaling instinct of keeping a thick body for less variability: thin the access-transistor body to ~2 nm Si (vertical fin or nanosheet), which raises the effective bandgap ~0.2-0.3 eV by quantum confinement. Band-to-band tunneling and thermal generation currents fall exponentially with the gap, and DRAM's modest on-current need absorbs the mobility loss.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): ~10-100x lower GIDL/generation current stretches retention several-fold at the same Cs.

title: Leakage becomes the latch: tunnel-diode Goto pair on storage node
idea: Reverse leakage from enemy to keeper: stack two nanoscale Esaki (interband tunnel) diodes in series between VDD and ground with the storage node at their midpoint. Their negative differential resistance creates two stable node voltages held by valley-current tunneling, so the node never drifts and the access transistor is only used to read and write.
why: Refresh disappears (fact 3) if diode valley current is <1 pA (otherwise static power rivals refresh); diodes stack vertically on the node, reviving the old TSRAM idea with modern Ge/Si tunnel junctions.

title: Move the data, not the amplifier: circulating CCD ring memory
idea: Reverse the access pattern: store bits as charge packets in short rings (32-64 positions) of buried-channel charge-transfer gates, so each packet passes a regenerating sense amplifier once per lap (~20-30 ns at 2 GHz during traffic, slowed to a crawl when idle). Refresh happens on every lap, random access waits at most one lap, and the buried channel under each gate is the storage well, so no capacitor pillar is needed.
why: Makes refresh intrinsic (fact 3) and removes the capacitor (facts 1, 2); latency stays in the 10-30 ns DRAM class; clocking energy and ~2-3 gates per bit are the risks.

title: Inside-out cell: access transistor grown inside the capacitor's hollow core
idea: Rearrange inside and outside: form the cylindrical storage capacitor first as an open shell, then grow a vertical gate-all-around channel up its hollow core so the capacitor's inner electrode is the transistor's drain, with no landing pad or buried contact between them. The wordline wraps the channel inside the cylinder.
why: Removes the storage contact/landing pad, a dominant leakage and resistance site (facts 3, 7), and folds transistor into capacitor footprint (~4F2), improving both retention tail and area.

title: Pay at write, not at refresh: pre-emphasized writes for weak rows
idea: Reverse when weak cells are compensated: a per-bank retention map fused at test flags the ~0.1-1% weak rows, and whenever such a row is written or restored, the bitline restore level is boosted 150-250 mV for a few ns. The extra charge carries weak cells to the nominal interval instead of refreshing whole banks at the weak-cell rate.
why: Refresh rate is set by the tail (fact 3); boosting ~1% of rows lets the bulk period double (64 to 128+ ms) for <1% extra energy, with dielectric stress confined to a few rows.

title: Bit-plane layout: MSB planes refresh fast, LSB planes rarely
idea: Rearrange tensor layout: transpose AI weights and activations into bit-planes so each DRAM row holds one significance level, then give sign/MSB rows normal refresh and the lowest 3-4 bit-plane rows 8-16x slower refresh. Rare decay flips in LSB planes perturb values by less than quantization noise, which models already tolerate.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3) for AI memory drops ~40-50% (half the planes at 1/8 rate); needs only per-region refresh rates.

title: Refresh by relocation shuffles row-hammer adjacencies every window
idea: Reverse refresh from restore-in-place into move: each refresh slot copies one row into a spare row in the same subarray (in-array row copy through the shared sense amps) and updates a small remap table, so within each window every row is both refreshed and physically relocated. An attacker can no longer keep hammering the same physical neighbors, so extra target-row refreshes become unnecessary.
why: Merges regular and mitigation refresh (facts 3, 9), recovering ~10-30% of refresh-related bandwidth at ~1k hammer thresholds for ~1 spare row per subarray.

title: Store less charge to keep more: low-field hold during self-refresh
idea: Reverse the instinct to store maximum charge: in self-refresh, restore '1's to ~0.7 V instead of ~1.0 V and set plate and negative wordline so the gate-to-storage-node field is minimal. GIDL and trap-assisted tunneling fall exponentially with field while charge falls only ~30%, so GIDL-limited tail cells hold longer; one full-swing pass restores normal margin on wake.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3, 16-33% of idle): if tail leakage drops >3x for 30% less charge, the interval can double while each refresh costs ~50% less CV2 energy (fact 10).

title: Reference cells that decay alongside their row
idea: Flip the sensing reference from a fixed VARY/2 to a moving one: each row carries a '1' and a '0' reference cell written at the same instant as the data and leaking through identical devices, and their charge-shared average becomes that row's sense threshold. As stored '1's sag, the threshold follows them down instead of waiting for them to cross a fixed midpoint.
why: Retention (fact 3): tracking common-mode decay tolerates ~2x more charge loss, giving ~1.5-2x longer refresh for ~0.03% area (2 cells per 8k).

title: Resonant wordline tank recycles refresh wordline energy
idea: Reverse the energy flow of refresh: because refresh activates rows in a fixed, known sequence, drive the boosted wordlines from an on-die LC tank (thin-film inductor in top metal) that swings each wordline up and returns its charge to the tank on the way down, instead of dumping pumped VPP charge to ground every row.
why: Refresh energy (facts 3, 10): wordline and charge-pump losses at VPP~3 V are a large share of refresh energy; recovering ~50-70% of them cuts refresh energy ~20-30% and shrinks VPP pump area (fact 7).

title: Negative-capacitance gate stack sharpens the access transistor's off-switch
idea: Reverse the sign of capacitance: add a thin ferroelectric layer tuned for negative-capacitance operation in series with the access transistor's gate oxide, so the internal gate voltage amplifies the wordline swing and subthreshold slope drops below 60 mV/dec. Vt can then be raised ~150 mV for leakage with no loss of on-current and no higher wordline voltage.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3) ~10x lower at equal Ion, relaxing refresh; or equal leakage at ~0.5 V lower wordline, easing the voltage floor (fact 10).

title: Power-switch fabs make memory switches: SiC-access DRAM tier
idea: Reverse the role of a power transistor: run underused 150/200 mm 4H-SiC MOSFET lines (idle after the EV slowdown) at their finest ~0.35-0.5 um rules to make 1T1C cells with SiC access transistors and trench capacitors. SiC's 3.3 eV gap gives intrinsic carrier density ~1e-9 cm-3, so off-current is low enough that retention reaches minutes to hours, as 1990s SiC DRAM demonstrations showed.
why: Uses existing SiC fabs (several in the U.S.) with no EUV to make a near refresh-free DRAM-class tier (fact 3); density is ~100x below leading DRAM, so it serves idle-dominated capacity, not bulk.

title: Sell the leaky dies: short-retention DRAM SKU for rewrite-heavy buffers
idea: Reverse the binning logic: dies that fail the 64 ms retention spec but pass at 8-16 ms, today scrapped or downgraded, become a 'fast-turnover' SKU for buffers that rewrite every row within milliseconds (AI activation and KV staging, video frames, packet buffers). The controller enforces a per-row touch deadline instead of refresh.
why: Raises usable supply from existing fabs by recovering retention-fallout yield (a few % of output) with no new tools, and drops refresh where it is wasted (fact 3).

title: Let the workload refresh: skip REF when activations cover every row
idea: Reverse who refreshes: in LLM inference every weight row is activated each token (~10-50 ms), and every ACT/PRE already restores its row. The memory controller keeps a per-bank activation-coverage bitmap over the refresh window and withholds REF for banks that were fully covered, falling back to normal REF the moment coverage lapses, while still issuing row-hammer RFM commands; firmware only, on unmodified DDR5/HBM.
why: Removes most refresh energy and the 10-20% refresh bandwidth loss (fact 3) for weight-streaming AI memory; no fab, firmware on existing controllers.

title: DIMM buffer chip takes over refresh with per-row retention map
idea: Rearrange who owns refresh: at OSAT test, profile each die's per-row retention under hot, pattern-stressed conditions and store a compressed weak-row list in a 28 nm buffer/register chip on the DIMM. The buffer intercepts host REF commands, keeps the DRAM out of auto-refresh, and issues RAS-only (ACT/PRE) refreshes at 64 ms only to the ~1% weak rows and at 256 ms+ to the rest.
why: Multi-rate refresh cuts refresh energy and bandwidth ~60-75% (fact 3) on existing commodity DRAM using a trailing-node buffer die; VRT cells need a guard band.

title: Reverse the airflow: DIMMs breathe first, processors second
idea: Rearrange server layout so cold inlet air, or the first segment of the liquid cold-plate loop, crosses the DRAM before the CPUs/GPUs: DIMM banks move to the chassis front and accelerators sit downstream. DRAM hot spots drop from ~85-95 C to ~50-60 C.
why: Exits the >85 C double-refresh range and halves leakage per ~10 C, so refresh energy and bandwidth loss fall ~2-8x (fact 3); a chassis change, no fab.

title: Steer data into the discharged state on unmodified DRAM
idea: Flip data polarity from outside the chip: commodity DRAM mixes true-cell and anti-cell subarrays. Map them once per part number with retention tests, then have the controller XOR-invert data per address so zeros, the most common value, land as discharged charge in both cell types, replacing today's random scrambling with a polarity-aware mask.
why: Fewer charged cells means fewer cells that can fail, so ECC-protected refresh relaxes ~2x (fact 3); controller logic only, on existing chips.

title: Trim the tail: charge-trap access transistors programmed at test
idea: Reverse a flash technique into a DRAM fix: build access transistors with an ONO (SONOS) charge-trap gate stack in an existing 40-65 nm embedded-SONOS fab. At wafer test, measure each cell's retention and give the tail cells (~0.01-1%) a one-time program pulse that raises their Vt ~200 mV and cuts their leakage 10-100x, folding the tail into the bulk distribution.
why: Refresh is set by the tail (fact 3); trimming it allows 64 ms to ~256 ms+ refresh (4x+) on existing trailing-node eSONOS lines; wordline disturb of the trap layer is the risk.

title: Back-gate dynamic threshold on existing 22/28 nm FD-SOI lines
idea: Rearrange threshold control from fixed doping to a live back gate: build 1T1C eDRAM cells with MIM capacitors on existing 22FDX/28FDS FD-SOI processes, holding the array's back-gate well at strong reverse bias in hold (Vt +250-300 mV) and switching it to forward bias only for the subarray being accessed. The thin BOX also isolates the storage node from the substrate, so there is no storage-node junction leakage.
why: Hold off-current falls ~100x while access speed is preserved (fact 3), using foundry capacity available today (Dresden, Crolles, Malta NY).

title: Flip the wafer: backside deep-trench capacitors etched in MEMS fabs
idea: Rearrange front and back: finish access transistors and bitlines on the wafer front in a mature DRAM/logic line, bond to a carrier, thin to ~20-40 um, then use existing 200 mm MEMS-fab DRIE (>=50:1 Bosch etch) to cut deep capacitor trenches from the backside up to each storage node. The capacitor gets the full silicon thickness instead of competing with bitlines for front-side height.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): micron-deep backside trenches give 3-10x Cs at relaxed pitch, and retention scales with it (fact 3); uses idle MEMS/TSV capacity, not EUV.

title: Cross-gated 2T1C: select one cell, not a whole row
idea: Rearrange selection from row-wide to cross-point: in a retired 2x/3x nm DRAM line, give each cell two series access transistors, one on the row wordline and one on a column-select line, so only the cell at the crossing connects. In hold, leakage must cross two off devices in series, and opening a row no longer disturbs its unselected cells.
why: Leakage ~10x lower via stack effect (fact 3), half-select and row-hammer disturbance largely gone (fact 9), 128x page overfetch removed (fact 8); ~1.5-2x density loss is paid in old fabs with spare capacity.

title: Compact free memory into refresh-off segments
idea: Reverse the OS goal from spreading pages to packing them: a kernel compaction daemon migrates live pages out of the top DRAM segments whenever utilization falls, then switches those segments' refresh off using partial-array self-refresh or segment masking that LPDDR5/DDR5 already support.
why: Servers average ~40-60% DRAM utilization and phones idle with free memory; refresh-off empty segments cut refresh/idle power ~30-50% (fact 3); software only.

title: Make refresh opt-in in the JEDEC standard
idea: Reverse the default in the DRAM standard: define a 'host-guaranteed retention' mode in which the die's internal refresh counter is disabled and the host certifies every row is touched or refreshed within the window, backed by an on-die watchdog bitmap that raises an alert if any row ages out. This standardizes what coverage-based, multi-rate and placement-based controllers need from existing dies.
why: Unlocks 50-90% refresh savings (fact 3) across the installed fab base through a spec revision instead of new process technology.

title: Weak rows get the hottest-written data
idea: Reverse page placement: the OS uses a per-row retention map to put frequently rewritten pages (stacks, network buffers, KV-cache heads) onto the weakest rows, since every write restores them, and cold read-mostly pages onto the strongest rows. The refresh interval then follows the strong rows.
why: Weak rows are refreshed by the workload itself, so the global interval can stretch 2-4x (fact 3) with no extra refresh traffic; OS and controller change on existing DRAM.

title: Image-sensor pixels as memory: pinned-photodiode storage cells
idea: Reverse the image sensor: in existing 55-90 nm CMOS image sensor fabs, use a light-shielded pinned photodiode as the storage well, the transfer gate as the access device, and the floating diffusion plus source follower as an in-cell gain readout, with write-back through a reset/inject path. Pinned photodiodes show dark currents of ~1-10 e-/s, so a few-thousand-electron packet holds for minutes.
why: Near refresh-free retention (fact 3) on idle trailing-node CIS capacity; density ~1-3 Mb/mm2 limits it to a retention tier, while charge transfer in tens of ns stays DRAM-class.

title: Swap hydrogen for deuterium in the final DRAM anneal
idea: Reverse the isotope: in existing mature DRAM lines, replace the forming-gas hydrogen anneal that passivates interface and STI traps with a high-pressure (~20 atm) deuterium anneal in existing high-pressure anneal tools. Si-D bonds resist hot-carrier and thermal depassivation far better than Si-H, so fewer traps reactivate into the GIDL and variable-retention-time tail.
why: Leakage tail and VRT (fact 3): a 2-3x smaller tail relaxes refresh ~2x from a single process-step swap; D2 supply is not geographically concentrated.

title: Errors set the refresh rate: ECC-feedback refresh loop
idea: Reverse the control direction: instead of a fixed worst-case tREFI, the controller lengthens each bank's refresh interval stepwise while watching DDR5 on-die ECC error-check-and-scrub counts and its own ECC syndromes, and backs off as soon as corrected errors per row exceed a threshold far below correction capacity. The memory reports its real retention instead of the datasheet predicting it.
why: Most dies retain 4-10x longer than spec at real temperatures, so refresh energy and bandwidth fall ~50-75% (fact 3); firmware on existing DDR5.

title: Qualify DRAM cold: a liquid-cooled retention grade
idea: Rearrange the spec around the deployment: create a datasheet grade qualified at <=55 C case temperature for direct-liquid-cooled racks, where retention is ~8x longer than at 85 C. Dies that fail 85 C retention screening but pass at 55 C enter this grade instead of downgrade or scrap, and all parts in the grade run 2-4x slower refresh.
why: Raises usable supply from existing fab output by recovering retention fallout and cuts refresh energy (fact 3); a test-flow and spec change only.

title: Elastic twin-cell rows: trade capacity for retention on demand
idea: Reverse one-cell-per-bit into two-cells-per-bit at run time: a decoder change in DRAM built on existing mature lines lets the controller pair a row with its twin across the open-bitline sense amps and store complementary charge, so the amplifier sees a full differential instead of a half signal. Regions switched to twin mode (phone standby, long-lived cold data) lose half their capacity but retain ~4-10x longer.
why: Self-refresh power in idle regions (fact 3) drops 4-10x; design-only change in existing DRAM fabs.

title: Reverse the e-waste flow: profile and redeploy retired server DRAM
idea: Flip decommissioned DIMMs from shredder back to rack: test pulled DDR4/DDR5 modules on existing ATE for per-row retention and error history, sort them into retention grades, and redeploy them in CXL memory-expander pools whose controller applies per-row multi-rate refresh and assigns weak rows to spare or short-lived buffer duty.
why: Raises usable memory supply with zero fab capacity (hyperscalers retire many PB per year) while retention-graded refresh keeps energy per bit acceptable (fact 3).

title: Tail bounty: pay for decades of worst-cell leakage cut
idea: Reverse the research metric from median to tail: a CHIPS-funded open prize pays per decade of 1-ppm-tail off-current reduction, measured on standard 1 Mb access-transistor test arrays built on shared 130/65 nm multi-project-wafer shuttles at existing U.S. foundries. Winning device recipes are licensed to DRAM makers.
why: Targets the ~13 fA tail that sets refresh (fact 3) with many cheap university and startup experiments on existing trailing-node shuttles instead of new fabs.

title: Swap 3D NAND roles: depreciated NAND lines build 3D DRAM
idea: Reverse 3D NAND's roles in a depreciated 64-96-layer NAND line: deposit alternating thin poly-Si and oxide planes as usual, but fill the vertical hole with metal as a wordline gate wrapping each plane, so each plane segment becomes a lateral access transistor whose far end is recessed and filled with a lateral MIM capacitor. The <=5 nm poly planes are fully depleted, and laser anneal enlarges grains to cut leakage.
why: Attacks 'no manufacturable 3D DRAM' (fact 2) and capital intensity (fact 4) on depreciated NAND tools with no EUV; poly-channel leakage limits retention, so it suits a dense short-refresh tier.

title: Ephemeral-memory cloud instances priced below standard RAM
idea: Reverse the memory guarantee into a product: cloud providers sell VM memory under a published 'touch-within-N-ms' contract (data preserved only if accessed or rewritten within, say, 32 ms) at a discount. These instances run on refresh-relaxed or refresh-off DRAM, including short-retention bins, and suit streaming inference, ETL and video pipelines that rewrite buffers continuously.
why: Monetizes refresh-free operation (fact 3) and lets lower-grade existing DRAM count as sellable capacity; a pricing and scheduler change, no fab.

title: Retention-first respin of a legacy DRAM node
idea: Reverse the optimization target on a fully depreciated 2x/3x nm DRAM line: give up ~30% density and spend the area on a longer recessed channel, thicker gate oxide at the storage-node overlap and a fatter capacitor, so the leakage tail drops ~10x and Cs rises ~1.5x. The part ships with ~1 s refresh as a low-idle-power LPDDR or CXL capacity tier.
why: Self-refresh power (fact 3) falls ~15x, and a paid-off line (depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost, fact 4) keeps cost per bit competitive despite lower density.
